summary: Describes IS-IS extensions for Multiprotocol Label Switching and GMPLS traffic engineering across multiple autonomous systems. It defines how to flood traffic engineering information about inter-AS links so that inter-AS path computation can work. It does not flood information from one AS into another. It was replaced by RFC 9346.

eli5.summary: Planning a trip across several countries needs maps of the border crossings. This describes how to share information about those crossings. It has been replaced by RFC 9346.

questions: how routers advertise inter-as te links
subtitle: How routers announce traffic engineering links across AS boundaries for path planning.

tldr.problem: When computing paths across multiple autonomous systems, routers need to know which neighboring ASes they can reach via traffic engineering links and what properties those links have.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new TLV for IS-IS routing to advertise information about inter-AS traffic engineering links, including the remote AS number and remote router identifiers, without flooding internal routing information between ASes.
tldr.outcome: ASes can now compute optimized paths that span multiple domains, supporting both per-domain path computation and cooperative PCE-based methods. It was superseded by RFC 9346.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering Across Boundaries
sections.content:
The IS-IS routing protocol, enhanced with traffic engineering (TE) extensions, allows routers within an autonomous system (AS) to advertise the capabilities of links and compute optimized paths. However, when traffic needs to cross multiple ASes, the entry point of each AS needs to know which exit points can reach the next AS, and what the link quality is.

This RFC extends IS-IS to advertise inter-AS TE links—the connections that cross from one AS to another—using a new TLV (Type-Length-Value field) without violating the fundamental principle that routing information stays within each AS.
sections.eli5: Each country has internal maps. This says how to mark borders so path-finders can see which countries connect, without sharing the internal maps.

sections.title: Why Inter-AS TE Information Is Needed
sections.content:
Two common scenarios require this information:

Per-domain path determination: When an entry router in an AS receives a path request destined for another AS, it must select which of its exit routers can reach that destination AS and choose the best one based on link quality (available bandwidth, delay, etc.).

Backward Recursive Path Computation (BRPC): When Path Computation Elements cooperate across domains, downstream PCEs return a tree of candidate paths to upstream PCEs. To correlate these paths, the PCE needs to know the identities of the exit routers in remote ASes and their connectivity, including the quality of inter-AS links.
sections.eli5: When choosing a border crossing, you need to know which crossings exist, where they lead, and whether the road is good or crowded.

sections.title: The Inter-AS Reachability TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new TLV type 141 (the Inter-AS Reachability TLV) that advertises inter-AS TE links. Unlike the standard IS reachability TLV, it contains:

  • The Router ID of the announcing router (the local ASBR)
  • Default metric and control bits (like the flooding scope flag)
  • Sub-TLVs that carry specific information:

Three key sub-TLVs are defined:

  • Remote AS Number (type 24): The AS number of the neighboring system
  • IPv4 Remote ASBR ID (type 25): The IPv4 address of the remote router
  • IPv6 Remote ASBR ID (type 26): The IPv6 address of the remote router

Existing TE sub-TLVs (bandwidth, delay, affinities) can be included to describe link properties. The RFC also defines two new sub-TLVs for the IS-IS Router Capability TLV to carry TE Router IDs across the entire routing domain when needed.
sections.eli5: The message says: 'This border crossing connects to AS 65000, where you can reach router 192.0.2.1, and it has 100 Mbps available.'

sections.title: Flooding and Procedures
sections.content:
When a router has a TE-enabled inter-AS link that is up, it advertises the link using the Inter-AS Reachability TLV. The TLV's flooding-scope bit controls whether the information stays within the local area or floods to the entire IS-IS routing domain.

Crucially, no IS-IS adjacency is formed on inter-AS links and no Hellos are exchanged. The advertising router acts as a proxy for the remote router, generating LSAs (Link State Advertisements) that describe both directions of the link so that path computation entities can do bidirectional checks.

The information source is the ASBR's knowledge of the link capabilities plus configuration. Legacy routers that do not understand the new TLV simply ignore it and continue flooding the LSP without using the information.
sections.eli5: A router announces its border crossing to all neighbors. It doesn't form a friendship with the other side—it just tells everyone what it knows about that crossing and what it can reach.

sections.title: Security and Constraints
sections.content:
The RFC is designed to respect the fundamental security model of IS-IS: there is no inter-AS information exchange, no flooding of information from one AS to another, and no change to inter-AS security relationships.

Since no ISIS adjacency forms on inter-AS links, the existing IS-IS authentication mechanisms (cleartext passwords or HMAC-MD5) secure the links. However, the remote AS number and remote ASBR ID are typically obtained manually from the neighboring operator. Care must be taken to verify this information before configuring it. BGP peering, if present, can help detect configuration inconsistencies.
sections.eli5: Each AS stays in control of its own security. The border information must be carefully checked because it comes from outside.
